message:
MESSAGE:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.

REQUESTS:
1. Explain what 'lippage' means in tiling
2. Suggest a grout colour for pale grey porcelain tile
3. Say whether to tile before or after fitting the new toilet, with a reason
4. Calculate how many boxes of 30x60 cm tiles (8 per box) are needed for a 2.4 x 1.8 m floor plus 10% waste  KEY: Area = 2.4 x 1.8 = 4.32 m^2; tile = 0.3 x 0.6 = 0.18 m^2, so 24 tiles exactly. Plus 10% = 26.4, round up to 27 tiles. 27/8 = 3.375, so 4 boxes (32 tiles). 3 boxes (24 tiles) is the no-waste shortcut and would leave them short. Answer: 4 boxes.
5. Write a short polite message to neighbours about tile-cutting noise
6. Give three tips for a beginner laying a floor

ANSWER:
Happy to help, and being a bit terrified is a good sign. It means you'll take your time.

## What "lippage" means

Lippage is when one tile's edge sits higher than the tile next to it, so you get a little lip you can feel underfoot or see when light hits the floor at an angle.

It's especially relevant to you because long rectangular tiles like 30 × 60 cm are often very slightly bowed in the middle. If you lay them half-overlapping like brickwork, the high middle of one tile lines up with the low ends of its neighbours and the lips get exaggerated. Two fixes:
- **Offset each row by a third of a tile (20 cm), not half.** Most tile makers recommend this for long tiles.
- **Use a tile levelling clip system.** These are cheap plastic clips and wedges that hold neighbouring edges flush while the adhesive sets.

## Grout colour

For pale grey porcelain, go **one or two shades darker than the tile**: a mid grey, often sold as "mid grey", "silver grey" or "pewter".
- White or very pale grout shows dirt within weeks, especially on a floor.
- Mid grey hides everyday grime and still looks neat against pale tiles.
- For extra protection, use a stain-resistant grout, or seal ordinary cement grout once it has cured.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Floor first, then the toilet.** The tiles run neatly under where the toilet sits, so there's no fiddly cutting around the base, and the toilet sits on a solid, level surface. It's also easier to swap the toilet later without leaving a gap in the tiles.

## How many boxes

| Step | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Floor area | 2.4 m × 1.8 m | 4.32 m² |
| Area of one tile | 0.3 m × 0.6 m | 0.18 m² |
| Tiles to cover the floor | 4.32 ÷ 0.18 | 24 tiles |
| Plus 10% | 24 × 1.1 = 26.4, round up | 27 tiles |
| Boxes of 8 | 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, round up | **4 boxes (32 tiles)** |

**Buy 4 boxes.** Three boxes would be exactly 24 tiles with nothing to spare, and you will need cuts even though the room happens to divide neatly into tiles. Walls are rarely perfectly straight, and the one-third offset leaves cut pieces at the row ends. The extra tiles are also useful for practising cuts, and keeping two or three afterwards means you can replace a cracked tile later with an exact match.

When you buy, check that all four boxes have the same **batch or shade number** printed on them, because colour can vary slightly between batches.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi both,
>
> Just a quick heads-up that I'll be cutting tiles for our bathroom floor this Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise from the tile saw, roughly 9:30 to 12:30. I'll keep it to the morning and try to get it done as quickly as I can.
>
> Thank you as well for putting up with the skip on the drive for the past couple of weeks. It should be gone very soon. If anything's causing you a problem, just knock.
>
> Thanks so much,
> [Your name]

Adjust the times to suit.

## Three tips for a first floor

1. **Preparation matters more than laying.** The floor underneath must be solid, clean and flat. Check it with a long straight edge, and fill any dips before you start. If it's a wooden floor, it needs a layer of plywood or tile backer board on top first. Most failed DIY floors fail because of what's underneath, not the tiling itself.

2. **Lay the tiles out dry before you mix any adhesive.** Arrange them on the floor without adhesive to plan where every cut will fall. Start from the centre line and adjust so you don't end up with a thin sliver of tile at the doorway or along the most visible wall. Ten minutes spent on this saves most of the "it looks a bit off" disappointment.

3. **Make sure the whole tile is stuck down.** Use a notched trowel with deep notches, around 10–12 mm, for tiles this size. Also spread a thin layer of adhesive on the back of each tile, called "back-buttering". Mix small batches so the adhesive doesn't start to set before you use it. After the first few tiles, lift one up to check that the back is almost fully covered. Tiles with hollow spots underneath are the ones that crack later.

Then stay off the floor for 24 hours before grouting. Good luck. A small, simple room like yours is a very sensible place to learn.
